title_candidates: Prompt injection is not just bad instructions - it is role confusion
summary: A new ICML paper argues that prompt injection works because models can treat hostile text as if it came from a trusted role.

primary_source.title: Prompt Injection as Role Confusion
primary_source.author: Charles Ye, Jasmine Cui, and Dylan Hadfield-Menell
key_facts: The paper argues that prompt injection comes from role confusion inside language models.
The authors test cases where untrusted text imitates roles such as user, tool, assistant, or reasoning text.
They report that the amount of role confusion can predict attack success before generation starts.
The paper was accepted to ICML 2026 and has been highlighted by Simon Willison as a useful explanation of prompt injection.

prerequisites: Any AI workflow that reads web pages, emails, documents, or tool output

steps.instruction: List every place where your agent reads untrusted text, such as web pages, tickets, emails, PDFs, or code comments.
For each source, ask whether the agent could mistake that text for an instruction.
Move permissions out of the prompt and into code, product settings, or human approval gates.
Test with a harmless fake instruction inside a document and confirm the agent ignores it.
Do not let an agent with private data browse untrusted text and send messages or run code without approval.
